title: SRE Standards: SLOs, Error Budgets, Capacity Planning, Reliability Initiatives, and Runbooks
author: Ari Chen
content:
Overview:

This document consolidates Redwood Inference's SRE standards for defining SLOs and error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives, incident review expectations, operational tooling, and runbook structure. It is intended for service owners, SREs, on-call engineers, and product teams who operate production inference services (hosted, dedicated, and private deployments).

Purpose:
- Provide a single, company-wide standard for measuring and governing reliability.
- Ensure consistent responses to SLO breaches and incidents.
- Define capacity planning cadence and minimum headroom targets.
- Standardize runbook format and incident review practices to drive measurable reliability improvements.

Scope:
- Applies to all production-facing services owned by engineering teams: API gateways, model-serving clusters, routing/selector services, KV/prefix caches, and observability pipelines.
- Exemptions must be approved by eng-sre and documented in the team's service catalog.

Definitions (quick):
- SLI (Service Level Indicator): a metric that captures user-perceived reliability (e.g., successful responses, p95/p99 latency).
- SLO (Service Level Objective): a target for an SLI over a rolling window (e.g., 99.95% availability per 30 days).
- Error budget: 1 - SLO; available budget to absorb unreliability without requiring immediate rollback.
- Burn rate: rate at which error budget is consumed.

SLO Ownership and Governance:
- Every production service must have an SLO document (page) linked from the team's service catalog.
- SLO owner: product or service owner (primary), on-call SRE (secondary).
- Quarterly SLO review: owners must review SLOs, SLIs, and alert thresholds with eng-sre.
- SLO changes: must be approved in a short RFC and coordinated with eng-sre for instrumentation and dashboards.

Recommended SLOs (examples):
- Serving API (customer-facing text completion):
  - Availability SLO: 99.95% successful request rate (HTTP 2xx) over 30d.
  - Latency SLO: p99 server-side request latency < 300ms for small requests (<=128 tokens) over 30d.
- Embeddings endpoint: 99.9% availability, p95 latency < 150ms.
- Control-plane operations (deploys, config API): 99.99% availability.

SLO example table (text):
- Service: model-serving-api | SLI: successful responses | SLO: 99.95% (30d) | Measurement: traffic-weighted rolling 30d
- Service: model-serving-api | SLI: p99 latency (<=128 tokens) | SLO: < 300ms (30d) | Measurement: rolling 30d

Error Budget Policy and Burn Guidance:
1) Status levels (percent of monthly error budget burned):
   - Green: 0-25% : Normal operations. Continue feature rollouts.
   - Watch: 25-75% : Reduce non-essential changes; increase monitoring frequency.
   - Restrict: 75-100% : Freeze non-critical releases; require SRE approval for changes.
   - Exhausted: >100% : Immediate mitigation required: consider rollbacks, enable fallbacks, mitigate root cause.
2) Calculation: error budget = (1 - SLO) * window_requests. Burn measured hourly and reported to the SRE dashboard.
3) Actions on sustained burn (>3 hours in Restrict):
   - Convene an incident command (IC) call and assign an incident lead.
   - Deploy mitigations: increase capacity (scale up), route traffic to lower-latency variants, enable degraded features (read-only, reduced sampling).
   - Post-incident: full incident review and corrective roadmap item within 7 days.

Capacity Planning (process and minimums):
- Cadence: Monthly capacity review and quarterly long-term forecasting.
- Forecast inputs: historical RPS (30/90/180d), sequence length distribution, model choice (FP16 vs int8), tail latency trends, sales/marketing events, and committed Dedicated capacity.
- Minimum operational headroom: 20% free capacity for normal operations; during high-risk events (product launch) increase to 30-40%.
- Capacity calculation (example, simplified):
  - Measured tokens/sec per GPU (T) = benchmarked throughput for the model variant.
  - Forecast tokens/sec required = forecast_RPS * avg_tokens_per_request.
  - GPUs_required = ceil(forecast_tokens/sec / T) + buffer (20%).
- Autoscaling policy guidance: keep fast scale-up paths (seconds-to-2-minutes) for serving tier and slower scale-down (10-30 minutes) to reduce oscillation.

Reliability Initiatives and OKRs:
- Initiative examples for each quarter:
  - Reduce p99 latency for small completions by 25% via kernel improvements and caching.
  - Ship automatic KV/prefix cache persistence to reduce cold-start exacerbations.
  - Improve observability: add end-to-end tracing for 90% of request paths.
- Tracking: reliability initiatives should be tracked as deliverables in the team roadmap with clear success criteria and linked to SLO improvements and cost estimates.

Incident Review and Postmortem Standards:
- Blameless culture: postmortems are facts-first and focused on systemic fixes.
- Timelines:
  1) Initial incident summary published within 24 hours.
  2) Draft postmortem within 72 hours.
  3) Final postmortem with action items and owners within 7 days.
- Required postmortem sections (flat list in the doc):
  - Summary and impact (customers, SLOs, error budget usage).
  - Timeline of events.
  - Root cause(s).
  - Contributing factors.
  - Immediate mitigations and why they worked/didn't.
  - Long-term corrective actions with owners and due dates.
  - Follow-up verification plan (how will we measure that the fix worked).
- Severity classification: Sev1 (customer-facing outage, >1 hour or significant revenue impact), Sev2 (partial degradation, intermittent errors), Sev3 (minor, localized). Severity determines SLA with exec communications and postmortem routing.

Operational Tooling (minimum required):
- Alerting: PagerDuty for paging; escalation policies per service (primary -> secondary -> engineering lead).
- Metrics: Prometheus (service metrics) + Datadog for aggregated dashboards and alerts.
- Tracing: Honeycomb or Jaeger for top-level request traces.
- Logs: Centralized ELK (Elasticsearch / Kibana) with structured logs and standardized fields (request_id, model_variant, customer_id (hashed), route).
- Error reporting: Sentry for control-plane errors and customer-facing SDK errors.
- Runbook/Playbook storage: Confluence (this namespace) and linked directly from PagerDuty incidents.
- Capacity and infra tooling: Terraform modules for GPU pool provisioning, autoscaling hooks connected to cluster-autoscaler or vaulted schedulers.

Runbook Standards and Template (mandatory fields):
- Runbook title (short).
- Service(s) covered.
- Owner/rotation/primary contact (PagerDuty schedule).
- Symptoms that should trigger this runbook (concrete metrics and thresholds).
- Immediate steps (1-3) for mitigation.
- Escalation steps (who to call, teams, and Slack channels).
- Post-incident tasks (data collection, logs to save, traces to sample).
- RPO/RTO expectations for actions.

Example runbook (model-serving-high-latency):
1) Symptom: p99 latency > 350ms for 5m AND error budget burn > 50% over 24h.
2) Owner: on-call Model Serving SRE (primary). PagerDuty: #models-oncall.
3) Immediate checks (5 minutes):
   - Check model-serving API dashboard (Datadog): request rate, p50/p95/p99 latencies.
   - Check GPU pool utilization (Grafana): node-level GPU % and memory pressure.
   - Verify recent deploys in the last 60 minutes.
   - Check routing service for uneven traffic distribution.
4) Mitigations (ordered):
   - If GPU utilization > 85%: scale up GPU pool (manual scale via terraform-runbook or trigger autoscale).
   - If a recent deploy occurred: roll back to previous stable revision.
   - Route a fraction of traffic to a cheaper/lower-latency model variant (feature-flagged fallback).
   - Enable degraded mode: reduce max tokens, disable non-essential telemetry sampling.
5) Notifications: post to #incident-model-serving and notify product owner and eng-sre lead.
6) If unresolved after 30 minutes: declare Sev2 and follow full incident process (assign incident commander, scribe, and communications lead).
7) Post-incident: collect heapdumps/profiles, export traces for the incident window, start postmortem draft within 72h.

Rollouts and Canary Guidance:
- Canary by request/sample: begin with 1% traffic, observe SLO metrics for 2x median request window (minimum 30 minutes).
- Automatic guardrails: canary must not increase error budget burn rate by >10% relative to baseline.
- Gradual ramp: 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100% with at least 30m observation at each step unless safety triggers fire.

Metrics and Dashboards (must-haves):
- Service-level SLI dashboard with: successful request rate, p50/p95/p99 latency, error budget remaining, traffic volume, deployment history.
- Infrastructure dashboard: GPU utilization, GPU memory pressure, node failures, queue lengths.
- Alert runbook links embedded in every alert.

Compliance and Reporting:
- Monthly SRE report: high-level SLO compliance, incidents, top reliability initiatives, and capacity changes.
- Executive summary sent quarterly to Product leadership and Finance for capacity spend alignment.

Appendix: Quick checklist for on-call engineers:
- Check alerts and dashboards immediately on page.
- Triage within 5 minutes and assign initial priority.
- Apply quick mitigations to protect customer experience (scales, fallbacks, rollbacks).
- Communicate every 30 minutes until mitigated.
- Complete postmortem template within the 72-hour window.
